# Restorative Agrisolar Design {.unnumbered}

::: {.draft-note}
**Working draft, circulated for comment.** Some citations are
[not yet verified](chapters/sources.qmd) and are marked where they appear, and the
[evidence base](chapters/evidence-and-needs.qmd) says what is established, what is
inferred, and what nobody has measured.
:::

::: {.welcome}
Solar and farming want the same flat, open, well-drained ground. An array can sit on pollinator habitat or on gravel. It can slow the water leaving a field or send it somewhere new, shade a flock, end the pumping on an irrigated field, or keep a farm in business. Which of those happens is a design decision.

[**Agrisolar**](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-agrisolar) is any solar on farmland or among it, including arrays that keep a farm producing or bring farming to ground that never had it, whether or not anything grows under the panels. [**Agrivoltaics**](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics) is the narrower case, where crops or livestock share the ground inside the fence. Growing crops directly under panels makes up less than two percent of what has actually been built, yet it gets a large share of the research attention [@stid2022; @macknick2022]. This lexicon is mostly about the other ninety-eight percent, and it tries to describe them just as precisely.

Where you draw the line decides what counts. Most accounting stops at the fence, the tops of the panels, and a meter into the soil. This lexicon draws the line around the farm and the community hosting the array instead, so the lease that keeps a farm solvent, the water leaving the field, and the habitat next door all count.

[**Restorative agrisolar design**](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-restorative) is the idea that a solar project's goals should include the soil, the water, the wildlife, and the neighbors, alongside the power it makes. This lexicon gives that idea words precise enough to test on a real site.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .running-example icon=false title="Rabbit Hills Solar Farm: A Restorative Agrisolar Example"}
![The pasture between the rows, grazed by the university's sheep. The instruments belong to the study that measured it. Photo from @adeh2018, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).](figures/photo_rabbit_hills.jpg){fig-alt="A grassy aisle runs between two long rows of solar panels mounted on steel posts, with a weather mast in the middle distance and oak trees and a hill beyond."}

On the Oregon State University campus in Corvallis, 1.4 megawatts of solar stand on six acres of what was a non-irrigated sheep pasture, and the university's sheep still graze it. Two peer-reviewed studies have measured what the array did. Through a dry summer the ground under the panels stayed wetter than the open pasture, and lambs raised there grew as fast as lambs in the open [@adeh2018; @andrew2021]. Each chapter of the primer places Rabbit Hills on its own scheme, in a box like this one, so that by the last chapter the array has a full description. It illustrates the vocabulary, and it is not an audit of the project.
:::

## A shared language

Put a [solar grazier](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-rangevoltaics), a township planner, a hydrologist, and a developer on the same eighty acres and you will get four descriptions that barely overlap. Those descriptions are being argued over right now, mostly without good information. Townships write ordinances with no comparable projects to learn from, and several states have taken permitting decisions away from the communities that host the arrays [@susskind2022; @bessette2024]. Shared words will not settle those arguments. They can help people find out what they are actually arguing about.

None of this is hypothetical. Around 15,000 ground-mounted arrays already cover some 3,000 km² of the United States. Roughly half of that ground was cropland before the panels went up, and another third was pasture or other farm grassland [@stid2022; @sturchio2025croplands]. A net-zero grid by 2050 could put solar on 60,000–90,000 km², about 1% of the lower 48 [@larson2021]. Most of that will be farmland too.

## How to read this lexicon

The lexicon comes in two parts. **Part I, the primer, is meant to be read straight through, in about half an hour.** Its seven chapters each answer one question, and each is built the same way: the answer in the first paragraph, one figure, one table naming every member of the scheme, and Rabbit Hills placed on it. Part II is looked up rather than read. It holds the [terminology](chapters/terminology.qmd), the full [archetype catalog](chapters/archetype-catalog.qmd), the [evidence base](chapters/evidence-and-needs.qmd), and the [sources](chapters/sources.qmd).

| | The question | The chapter that answers it |
|---|:--|:--|
| **1** | What choices do designers have for shaping the array? | [Design Levers](chapters/design-levers.qmd): six kinds of choice |
| **2** | What forces push on the array's design? | [Design Pressures](chapters/design-pressures.qmd): nine forces |
| **3** | How large is the array? | [The Scale Transect](chapters/scale-transect.qmd): five size zones, A1 to A5 |
| **4** | What happens to farming on the ground the array takes? | [The Farming Axis](chapters/farming-axis.qmd): six positions, S0 to S5 |
| **5** | Which choices do the restorative work? | [Restorative Work](chapters/restorative-work.qmd): six leads, one per lever |
| **6** | How does the array affect the landscape? | [Restorative Functions](chapters/restorative-functions.qmd): four functions, eight outcomes |
| **7** | What does the practice look like on real ground? | [Archetypal Forms](chapters/archetypal-forms.qmd): thirteen recurring designs |
: The seven questions of the primer, and the chapter that answers each. {#tbl-questions}

The schemes fit together in one direction. The six [design levers](chapters/design-levers.qmd) are the choices designers have for shaping an array, and nine [design pressures](chapters/design-pressures.qmd) push on how each one gets set. Design levers do both design work, setting the form of the array, and restorative work, setting its impact. Once the levers are set, any project can be described three ways: how big it is, what happened to the farming on its ground, and which lever leads its restorative work. Those settings decide how the array affects the landscape around it, through its [restorative functions](chapters/restorative-functions.qmd). The designs that keep turning up on real ground are the [archetypes](chapters/archetypal-forms.qmd).

![How the pieces fit. **Top row:** the nine design pressures, grouped by which way they push, acting on the six levers. Each lever is colored by the [restorative work](chapters/restorative-work.qmd) it can lead. **Bottom row:** what a set of choices produces: a place on the scale transect and on the farming axis, the lever that leads the restorative work, and a footprint across the four kinds of outcome.](figures/fig_language_structure.svg){#fig-language-structure}


::: {#sec-aim-not-dimensions}
**This lexicon argues for an aim and leaves the dimensions to the site.** It takes a clear position on what agrisolar is *for*. It does not say how high to raise the panels or how far apart to set the rows, because the same choices that restore ground in one region can wear it down in another.
:::

## How sure we are

The claims in this lexicon rest on evidence of very different strength. Grassland birds are more abundant on planted solar sites than on the farmland around them, and that is known because people counted them [@walston2025]. That a seeded ground layer keeps sediment out of the creek below is the prairie-strip result from corn and soybean fields [@schulte2017], carried over onto ground nobody has sampled under an array. The sentences making those two claims look alike. The [evidence base](chapters/evidence-and-needs.qmd) says once which is which, so the chapters do not hedge every sentence. The largest open questions are whether several mid-sized arrays do more than one large one, which decides how much restorative work scale does, how much soil construction costs a site, and whether a restorative planting outlasts routine maintenance.

## Joining in {#sec-joining}

The most useful thing anyone can send is an account of a real project, working or not. The
[Describe a project](https://github.com/MSUHydrogeology/restorative_agrisolar_lexicon/issues/new?template=describe-a-project.yml) form asks what the ground was
before, what changed, who runs it, what was promised, what was measured, and what did not work.
Corrections, counterexamples, and proposed terms are welcome as issues or pull requests on
[GitHub](https://github.com/MSUHydrogeology/restorative_agrisolar_lexicon). Especially useful: an archetype
that recurs in your region and is missing here, a term that lands badly with the people who have
to use it, or a citation you can trace further than we have.
